## Highlights

**WireGuard and AmneziaWG keys are now detected.** The new contextual rule `wireguard-key-assignment` reports a preshared or private key under its key name: in wg/awg configuration (`PresharedKey = …`, `PrivateKey = …`), YAML and JSON variables, Python reprs, JSON escaped into JSON strings (as in ansible failed-task output), JSON-printed command output and `--psk=…` flags. The rule is on by default and applies in the pre-commit scan, in `audit`, and in the `redact-claude` and `check-codex` agent hooks. Masking replaces only the key; the key name and the syntax around it stay visible.

## Upgrade notes

The new rule is on by default, so a commit that adds such a key is now blocked and agent output that holds one is masked. To turn the rule off, set `"wireguard-key-assignment" = false` under `[settings.rules]`.

Upgrade: `brew upgrade vshuraeff/tap/sekretbarilo`, then `sekretbarilo doctor`.

## Changes

### Detection

- New rule `wireguard-key-assignment`, contextual and enabled by default.
  - **Key name.** One of `psk`, `preshared key` or `private key`, either on its own or as the end of a longer snake, kebab or camel name (`sops_amneziawg_awg0_psk`, `wireguard_private_key`, `peerPresharedKey`, `WGPrivateKey`). The name is also read after a `\n`, `\r` or `\t` escape.
  - **Value.** Exactly a WireGuard key: 43 base64 characters and one `=`.
  - **Not reported.** Public keys, `(hidden)` in `wg show` output, file paths, template references and values of any other shape.
- The rule checks only your own `[allowlist] stopwords`, and documentation files get no entropy bonus for it. The built-in stopwords and the bonus would drop a real random key about once in several hundred.
- A key is still reported when a template expression (`{{ … }}`) is on the same line.

### Counts

- 115 built-in rules, 111 of them enabled by default. 39 rules are contextual.
